writer_notes: Strongest material: (1) The Karlag and deportation story. The city was built partly by prisoners and deported peoples, and in the 1940s up to 70% of residents were ethnic Germans. Over 100,000 people later emigrated to Germany. Note that the 70% and emigration figures are [W] only. (2) Vivid survival details from independent sources: dugouts shared by 2–3 families [54], dung-fueled stoves [55], mass deaths in 1931–33 [52]. (3) The "Where? In Karaganda!" punchline and its 2011 monument, plus the Irtysh–Karaganda canal. All of these are [W] only, so present them as Wikipedia-sourced or keep them light. Flag or soften these disputed points: the coal discoverer (Baizhanov is "allegedly" the finder, the attribution is contested [3], and he was formalized as discoverer by a 1932 newspaper [2]); the first mine date (1856 vs 1857); the Karlag start date (1930 vs 1931); the 1939 population (~100,000 with half prisoners vs 166,000); and city rank (4th vs 5th). Avoid exact figures on these, or give the range. The nuclear EMP fire, the visa refusals to RFK and Douglas, and the near-capital story are [W]-only extras. The 2023 Kostenko disaster is corroborated [74] and gives the post a present-day stake.
has_angle_reason: This is a half-million-person city in the dry, cold central Kazakh steppe. Its name became a Soviet byword for the middle of nowhere: "Where?" — "In Karaganda!". The brief explains why people are there. Coal was found in the 1830s. Stalin then built a city to mine it, using Karlag slave labor and deported peoples (Volga Germans, Chechens, Crimean Tatars and others). Settlers dug their own dugouts and burned dung for fuel. Water had to be piped in by a 400+ km canal. Coal still sustains the city. That is a remarkable origin by decree and forced relocation, and the brief answers the question.
corroborated_reason: The central answer is coal plus forced labor. Both have web sources alongside [W]. Coal origin: "The city traces its origin to 1833, when a local shepherd... allegedly found coal on the site [W][1][25]." Forced labor: "The Karlag prison camp network was created to supply slave labor for the mines [21][W]." Coal remaining central today: "[42]" industrial hub for coal mining and metallurgy, and "26 mines in Soviet times and 8 as of 2023 [W][73]." The brief reports the disagreements on dates and on who discovered the coal rather than hiding them.
